a279.speaker: Swedish Radio's news program Ekot (investigation)
a279.speech: revealed that Sweden's ambassador in Mogadishu reached an agreement in December 2023 with Somalia's Prime Minister to redirect 100 million kronor from Sweden's aid budget into a Somali-Italian development fund; in return, Somalia would take back citizens that Sweden wanted to deport, including individuals convicted of crimes who refused to leave. According to Ekot, Somalia's government insisted on control over the funds through the prime minister's office.

a279.speaker: Analysts
a279.speech: say the move blurred lines between development support and political patronage.

a279.speaker: Omar Mahmood, Somalia analyst with the International Crisis Group
a279.speech: "This (deal) is an example of how the Somali government is trying to secure direct control over more resources," in an interview with Swedish Radio.

a279.speaker: Somali authorities
a279.speech: suspended deportations, accusing Sweden of breaching the agreement.

a279.speaker: Somali officials (anonymous)
a279.speech: told Ekot they viewed her [Sweden's aid chief Anna Saleem Hogberg] as "standing in the way of the money."

a279.speaker: Mats Harsmar, deputy director of Sweden's Expert Group for Aid Studies (EBA)
a279.speech: "The goals are vague and the indicators unclear. It's hard to know whether any outcomes were achieved."

a279.speaker: Wilo Abdulle Osman, Somali return migration specialist
a279.speech: "The risk of corruption is obvious to anyone who has worked on these issues."

a279.speaker: Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index
a279.speech: Somalia ranks second to last on Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index.

a279.speaker: Opposition lawmakers in Stockholm
a279.speech: have condemned the deal as irresponsible.

a279.speaker: Morgan Johansson, Social Democrats
a279.speech: "It is highly reckless to transfer such large sums into funds associated with Somalia's top leadership given the country's corruption levels," said Morgan Johansson, who demanded a parliamentary inquiry.

a279.speaker: The Center Party and Green Party
a279.speech: also denounced the agreement as "corruption and political misdirection."

a279.speaker: Anna Lasses, Center Party foreign policy spokesperson
a279.speech: told SVT the revelations were "deeply alarming."

a279.speaker: Benjamin Dousa, Minister for International Development Cooperation, Moderate Party
a279.speech: defended the policy, saying development aid can be used to promote migration objectives. "We expect our agencies to deliver on government policy," Dousa said. "It is reasonable to use aid as an incentive for countries to take back their citizens."

a279.speaker: SIDA officials
a279.speech: told Swedish media they felt political pressure from the government to proceed. The agency declined comment.

a279.speaker: UNDP
a279.speech: said the project complied with its standard accountability procedures.

a279.speaker: Public broadcaster Yle
a279.speech: reported that Helsinki set an informal target of 100 accepted deportees before reconsidering the freeze.

a279.speaker: Somali prime minister's office
a279.speech: Ekot said it sought comment from the Somali prime minister's office but received no response.

a335.speaker: Noutè Bamba, former soloist of the group Nimba Succès de Lola
a335.speech: “It all began with Bèrè Jazz, at Gama Bèrèma, 42 kilometres east of the urban commune. That is where I learned to play the guitar, with Koui Bamba, who was himself trained by the late Aboubacar Demba Camara.”

a335.speaker: Noutè Bamba, former soloist of the group Nimba Succès de Lola
a335.speech: “My father did not send me to school. For me, it was music that I loved” ; “Everything I earned, I put into Nimba Succès. Even the instruments the group still uses today, it was I who bought them.”

a335.speaker: Noutè Bamba, former soloist of the group Nimba Succès de Lola
a335.speech: Laments that the musicians now live in general indifference: “Even when we are sick, no one comes to see us. And yet we gave everything to make Lola and Guinea shine through music” ; launches a pressing appeal to the authorities, cultural officials, local authorities and civil society: “music united us. Today, we simply ask not to be forgotten” ; “it is music that made me known. It is music that gave everything to Lola.”

a339.speaker: Landless People’s Movement (LPM)
a339.speech: Is dissatisfied with the level and progression of decentralisation in Namibia; the party claims that the Ministry of Urban and Rural Development, which is responsible for the decentralisation function, is delaying the transfer of power to local authorities and regional councils.

a339.speaker: Ivan Skrywer, LPM Councillor
a339.speech: Said the government must empower local authorities to drive development and build lasting resilience against the challenges facing citizens; noted that while there has been a lot of talk in public forums, there hasn’t been much action on the ground.

a339.speaker: Ivan Skrywer, LPM Councillor
a339.speech: Expressed dissatisfaction with the proposed amendments to the Regional Councils Act, which govern the appointment of Chief Regional Officers. “He stated that appointments now require prior written approval from the minister based on recommendations from the PSC, as the president may resolve disputes. Now, all of a sudden, consultation with the minister is replaced with prior written approval, totally taking away the power of elected officials. Who, by the way, are paying these officials?” ; “You can’t appoint somebody that you’re not paying; that is the order of the day, and it should be the order of the day, and that is not the case with the current proposed amendments.”

a339.speaker: Evelyn Nawases-Taeyele, Deputy Minister (of Urban and Rural Development)
a339.speech: Stated in her speech during the Decentralisation Day that the government worked towards empowering Regional Councils and Local Authorities through legislative reforms and reviews, capacity building and fiscal resources, but said there is still a need to enhance the capacity of local institutions to manage resources effectively and transparently.

a568.speaker: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Malawi (communication)
a568.speech: According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ communication, Chakwera will be home on Saturday, October 5, 2024, with the plane expected to land at Kamuzu International Airport at 15:45 hours.

a568.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a568.speech: In his address during the General Assembly debate, the Malawi leader presented a case for UN Security Council reform, lobbying for not only inclusion of Africa in the Council but also veto powers, and mobilised global support for Malawi’s developmental priorities.

a568.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank (AfDB)
a568.speech: Announced the grant of MK95 billion to Malawi, of which MK1 billion is meant for the purchase of food for people affected by hunger through the Department of Disaster Management Affairs.

a671.speaker: Jerolinmek Piah, Minister of Information, Culture and Tourism of Liberia
a671.speech: Said the unveiling of the Arts and Culture Gallery signified the re-opening of the forgotten Cultural Promotion Chapter within the Ministry, noting that such feat would not have been achieved without the immense contributions of former Culture Ambassador Juli Endee ; "The unveiling of the rich Liberian arts and culture gallery is one the first steps towards the promotion of our cultural heritage. Cultural Promotion was given serious attention at MICAT from 1951 to 1990... The war and post war eras neglect seriously affected this important responsibility of MICAT." ; "Since the ascendency of me and my team in 2024, we continue to maintain and direct equal focus not only on government information dissemination, but also tourism development and cultural heritage promotion." ; "For this reason and with an excellent concept and breath-taking creativity of former Cultural Ambassador Queen Juli Endee, we embarked upon and now see this impressive display of our Liberia's rich cultural artefacts."

a671.speaker: Jerolinmek Piah, Minister of Information, Culture and Tourism of Liberia
a671.speech: Said the gallery gives one the feeling about how diverse and rich Liberia's cultural heritage is, and that MICAT will ensure the reactivation of the National Cultural Center and reorient the National Cultural Troupe: "Already, MICAT has pitched to UNESCO Headquarters in Paris through inter-ministerial collaboration with the Ministry of Education, the revamping, restocking and repositioning of our National Museum..." ; "These are the tasks we are embarking upon and with full and adequate support, the lost glory of this entity can and will be restored... Phase II will see the replacements of windows, doors, ceiling, reconditioning/building of restrooms, offices, floors, the fence, landscaping among others. Together, we can think, love and build our cultural diversities and richness to foster national unity and economic prosperity."

a671.speaker: Juli Endee, former Cultural Ambassador of the Republic of Liberia
a671.speech: Praised authorities at the Ministry of Information for always providing the platform for her involvement in promoting the country's rich arts and culture heritage: "It's always a pleasure to be here at the Ministry of Information, Cultural Affairs and Tourism. I've worked with past and present leaders of this Ministry." ; "As a traditional queen of the republic of Liberia, I am leaving within this Ministry very important artifacts of arts, culture and tourism. Creativity and imagination equal innovation. So, today we are here to unveil a dream. I want to thank my father Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr., who has given me the opportunity to serve as Commissioner General of the World Expo in Japan. I am also on the International World Expo Committee for Exhibition, and I will be taking Liberia to Japan."

a671.speaker: Kekura Kamara, Liberia's new Cultural Ambassador
a671.speech: Promised to use his platform to bring the government to the people, and informed of a new cultural roadshow planned for the first week in every February where Liberian culture will be displayed and the ARREST Agenda showcased through cultural performances.

a671.speaker: Christopher Onanuga, Special Presidential Envoy on Tourism
a671.speech: "I am overjoyed because tourism is the embodiment of growth in every sector of the economy in every nation. And when we pursue it, it shines the light. Ninety percent of tourists come to Africa. This time around for the next 200 years they will be coming only because of heritage purposes."

a671.speaker: Christopher Onanuga, Special Presidential Envoy on Tourism
a671.speech: Underscored the importance of the media in promoting tourism and called on the Fourth Estate to put up the plate for his national duty call: "The Fourth Estate has a critical role to play in selling tourism. Talk about it, let everybody know what's going on. When you look at the newspapers, the online TV, the websites, the TV, nothing is dedicated to tourism, the arts and culture."

a671.speaker: Bernard Blue Benson, Representative and Chair of the House Committee on Information, Broadcasting, Culture and Tourism
a671.speech: Said tourism cannot strive without an organized and functioning culture: "We support the reestablishment of Kendeja. If we are serious about tourism, the re-establishment of Kendeja must be prioritized. Kendeja serves as our cultural identity. Mr. Vice President, Senator Dillon, all members of this high table, we must put our hands together to reestablish Kendeja. If you are to be serious to boost Liberia to the world, the engine that serves as our cultural identity that has been destroyed must be reestablished."

a671.speaker: Abraham Darius Dillon, Senator and Senate Chairman on Information, Broadcasting, Culture and Tourism
a671.speech: Said the Liberian Senate in recent times concurred with the House of Representatives to pass into law the Tourism Act to give autonomy to the tourism industry: "As we speak the endorsed bill is on its way to the Executive Mansion for approval and printing into handbill. We did that on purpose because it is a legacy agenda of the Joseph Nyuma Boakai administration. We go to other countries; we see their tourism sectors booming... because deliberate concrete steps are taken towards achieving this goal." ; "Creation of the Tourism Commission is not sufficient. We must fund it. We will do everything to ensure there is budgetary support. We look forward to the Executive considering the latest action of the United States government when it comes to USAID" ; called on all government ministries and agencies to use the Liberia Broadcasting System to break all government news.

a671.speaker: Dr. Augustine Konneh, Advisor to the President
a671.speech: Said the unveiling of the arts and culture galleries is a true manifestation of Liberian culture, its inheritance, and heritage: "If you do not write about your own culture, your history; someone will write it for you. And if they write it for you, you will not like it."

a671.speaker: Oswald Tweh, Justice Minister of Liberia
a671.speech: Said the occasion was a milestone that all Liberians must be proud of: "Our cultural heritage is very important. When people come to your country, they don't come to see what they have, but what they don't have."

a671.speaker: Jeremiah Kpan Koung, Vice President of Liberia
a671.speech: Emphasized the importance of cultural preservation and tourism, reaffirming the significance of preserving Liberia's cultural heritage as a foundational pillar of the nation's identity and development, noting "culture cannot be overlooked" and calling for concerted efforts to safeguard and promote Liberia's cultural traditions ; noted the necessity of enhancing Liberian colloquialisms and integrating them into the national education system ; urged the government to prioritize investments in the tourism sector and called for the restoration of the iconic yet neglected Hotel Africa ; commended the Minister of Information, Cultural Affairs, and Tourism and expressed gratitude to the legislature for the recent passage of the Tourism Bill.

a671.speaker: Jeremiah Kpan Koung, Vice President of Liberia
a671.speech: Underscored the importance of investing in media, stating "Information dissemination remains crucial to the development process", and called for enhanced government support to strengthen media infrastructure and its role in promoting Liberia's cultural and economic initiatives.

a909.speaker: Stakeholders of the Integrated Health Services Activity (Ihsa) project
a909.speech: Welcome the convincing results obtained over five years of implementation (2018-2023) in the departments of Alibori, Atacora, Ouémé and Plateau.

a909.speaker: Brinille Eliane Ellis, Deputy Chief of Mission of the Embassy of the United States of America in Benin
a909.speech: Recalled that the Ihsa project, worth $22.5 million (about 13.9 billion CFA francs) and financed by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), aimed to strengthen local capacities to provide quality health care through high-impact services for malaria, family planning, maternal and child health, gender-based violence (GBV), and Covid-19 prevention and control; it is implemented by the international organisation Management Sciences for Health (MSH) in partnership with Dimagi and four local partners, namely Cerrhud, Ceradis, Dedras and Apessa, with strong engagement from the government and citizens.

a909.speaker: Brinille E. Ellis, Deputy Chief of Mission, US Embassy in Benin
a909.speech: Reiterated the commitment of the United States government to support Benin’s efforts in the health sector.

a909.speaker: Dr Enagnon Pétas Akogbéto, Chief of Staff of the Minister of Health
a909.speech: Is pleased, at the institutional level, with the establishment of a digital application called “AlafiaComm” for the management of community data; he also welcomed the development of the first model of a digital health map to facilitate decision-making, the updating of normative documents, guides and supervision tools, and the strengthening of the health system through donations of materials and equipment needed for emergency obstetric and neonatal care (EmONC) and for infection prevention and control, thanks to the project.

a909.speaker: Dr Floride Niyuhiré, Director of the project
a909.speech: Details that technical and financial support to the first malaria chemoprophylaxis campaign made it possible to protect 1.8 million children under 5 between 2019 and 2022; the supply of materials and equipment worth about 4 billion CFA francs strengthened the technical capacity of health facilities; and with the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic, the project made it possible to sensitise nearly 2 million people, of whom more than a million were vaccinated against the coronavirus.

a909.speaker: Dr Agnès Oladoun Badou Savi, Deputy Chief of Staff of the Minister of Social Affairs and Microfinance
a909.speech: Notes that alongside the Social Promotion Centres (CPS), the project supported GBV survivors by providing them with medical care, psychosocial support, judicial assistance and opportunities for socio-professional reintegration; she affirms the willingness of the Ministry of Social Affairs to maintain and strengthen the gains, including the operationalisation of the Computerised System of Data on the Family, Women and Children – New.

a983.speaker: Ismail Omar Guelleh, President of the Republic of Djibouti
a983.speech: “First of all, I would like to express my sincere thanks and deep appreciation to His Majesty King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, as well as to his government and his people, for their warm welcome, their generous hospitality and the remarkable preparation of this summit,” before also thanking His Majesty King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, His Royal Highness Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, and the Secretary General of the Arab League and his staff.

a983.speaker: Ismail Omar Guelleh, President of Djibouti and current Chairman of IGAD
a983.speech: Evoking Israel's continued aggression against the Gaza Strip, “exposing to the whole world the most horrific crimes against humanity”, he stressed: “Our meeting comes at a critical moment while the Arab region is confronted with unprecedented challenges.” ; “We recognise the gravity of this tragedy and call for a united Arab response to put an end to this war of extermination against our people in Gaza,” and insisted on an immediate and lasting ceasefire to protect civilians, to put “an end to forced displacement and ensure safe access to humanitarian aid”.

a983.speaker: Ismail Omar Guelleh, President of Djibouti
a983.speech: Said “the need to revive the peace process by supporting the two-State solution in accordance with international resolutions and by recognising Palestine as a full member of the UN, thus allowing the Palestinian people to realise their legitimate rights and establish an independent State with East Jerusalem as its capital” constitutes an absolute necessity to ensure a safe and prosperous future for all the peoples of the region.

a983.speaker: Ismail Omar Guelleh, President of Djibouti
a983.speech: Regarding the crises in Yemen, Libya and Sudan, called for “effective collective Arab action”: “If we do not cooperate to contain these crises, they risk being prolonged with disastrous consequences for Sudan and the region as a whole. Resolving these crises requires a collective and urgent effort, as I have stressed previously.” ; Emphasised “the efforts made by the Republic of Djibouti, notably within the framework of its rotating presidency of IGAD, to contribute to resolving the crisis in Sudan”, adding: “Djibouti reaffirms its welcome and its total support for all initiatives aimed at helping the Sudanese overcome this ordeal and find a comprehensive political solution to the crisis.”

a983.speaker: Ismail Omar Guelleh, President of Djibouti
a983.speech: On international division and polarisation, which have given rise to “a struggle for the imposition of divergent wills and the unequal application of international law”, declared: “we must turn to our own capacities”, underlining the importance “of strengthening our collaboration and unifying our efforts to develop decisive and radical solutions to the current and future challenges that threaten our nation”. ; “This will inevitably require the development and promotion of renewed Arab cooperation, adopting an innovative approach that puts the concerns of Arab citizens at the forefront of our priorities.”

a983.speaker: Ismail Omar Guelleh, President of Djibouti
a983.speech: Expressed his support for the candidacy of Mahmoud Ali Youssouf for the presidency of the African Union Commission, underlining the importance of African unity in the pursuit of the continent's development and prosperity.

a983.speaker: Ismail Omar Guelleh, President of Djibouti (bilateral meetings)
a983.speech: Underlined the importance of regional cooperation to address the security and humanitarian challenges affecting Libya and the region as a whole; expressed firm support for the transition process in Libya, underlining the crucial need to establish lasting stability for the well-being of the country and the region.

a983.speaker: Arab leaders (final declaration of the 33rd Summit of the Council of Arab States – Bahrain Declaration)
a983.speech: Reaffirmed their bonds of fraternity and shared history, underlining the importance of collective action to preserve the security and stability of the Arab States; expressed their commitment to peace, tolerance and peaceful coexistence while firmly condemning terrorism in all its forms; unequivocally condemned Israeli aggression against the Gaza Strip and urgently called for an end to this aggression, the lifting of the blockade and the entry of humanitarian aid; expressed solid support for Sudan, Syria, Yemen and Libya, calling for political solutions in line with the aspirations of their peoples; and committed to strengthening partnerships with international alliances and cooperating with the United Nations to meet global challenges, including achieving the sustainable development goals by 2030.

a1076.speaker: Shiri Keivon, new Ambassador of the Republic of India to Djibouti
a1076.speech: In a speech delivered on the occasion, expressed his delight at taking part in the signing of this partnership agreement, which promises to strengthen trade relations between India and Djibouti. "This is a great achievement for our two countries," he insisted.

a1076.speaker: Isse Abdillahi Assoweh, Ambassador of Djibouti to India
a1076.speech: Expressed his gratitude to the president of the Djibouti chamber of commerce for the warm welcome given to himself and to the Indian business delegation. He stressed that the public sector alone cannot support the population and that wealth comes from the private sector.

a1076.speaker: Youssouf Moussa Dawaleh, President of the Djibouti Chamber of Commerce
a1076.speech: Welcomed the Indian delegation to Djibouti and expressed his joy at taking part in this ceremony for the signing of an agreement between the Djibouti chamber of commerce and India. He then recalled Djibouti's economic potential and opportunities as well as investment exchanges, thanks to its privileged geostrategic position with a logistics, port, telecoms and modern infrastructure platform serving the region.

a1076.speaker: Youssouf Moussa Dawaleh, President of the Djibouti Chamber of Commerce
a1076.speech: Also praised the valuable efforts of the two embassies, India and Djibouti, for their hard work, which made this partnership agreement possible.

a1107.speaker: Environmental Investment Fund of Namibia (EIF) (statement)
a1107.speech: "Under the project 'Green, Resilient Recovery Rapid Readiness Support in Namibia' (NAM-RS-004), the EIF has commissioned Fichtner to assess the feasibility of producing green hydrogen and its derivatives in Namibia in the planned 'hydrogen valley' (the second after Luederitz). This central region comprises the three regions of Erongo, Khomas and Otjozondjupa." ; "It is envisaged that this region will become a 'hub' for the production of synthetic fuels and associated production facilities for green hydrogen equipment."

a1107.speaker: Christina Mansfeld, representative of Fichtner GmbH & Co.
a1107.speech: Gave an overview of everything the study covers, including solar and wind potential as well as production potential for hydrogen and hydrogen derivatives and the associated estimated production costs; "The study also aims to assess potential enablers for an economic and social integration of green hydrogen and derivatives for the central hydrogen valley."

a1107.speaker: Neville Andre, Governor of the Erongo Region
a1107.speech: "It is absolutely essential to include the cumulative negative and positive environmental impacts that arise from too many green hydrogen projects in one region."

a1125.speaker: Nnimmo Bassey, executive director of Health of Mother Earth Foundation
a1125.speech: Said the spill, which occurred on May 6, was yet to be stopped, adding that the slow response showed a lack of care for the people and was "unconscionable." ; "We are in a disaster zone and further disasters can erupt from even an accidental spark of fire." ; "The fact that this spill that happened a week ago is yet to be stopped sends a very strong point to why the government should focus on cleaning up Ogoniland and not seek to open new oil wells. The old wells should be shut down, and decommissioned."

a1125.speaker: Renaissance Group, Nigerian oil consortium
a1125.speech: Confirmed the explosion and said a team of investigators has been dispatched to determine the cause of the spill.

a1125.speaker: Trans Niger Pipeline (TNP)
a1125.speech: Did not immediately provide a statement when asked for comment.

a1472.speaker: John Mahama, President-elect of Ghana
a1472.speech: has reiterated his commitment to strengthen the historic ties between Ghana and the US ; mentioned energy, security and agriculture as some of the sectors that needed special attention to propel the country's growth ; "I want to tell you how much we look forward to working with you to deepen the Ghana-US partnership." ; "The relationship between our two countries is historic. I also want to thank you for the warm relations we have personally."

a1472.speaker: John Mahama, President-elect of Ghana
a1472.speech: acknowledged the comparative advantage the US has in technology and expressed his willingness to work closely with the US to resolve the challenges in Ghana's energy sector: "We know that we can tap into your knowledge in that sector. We want to work closely with you to resolve some of the issues in the energy sector," he said ; further highlighted the successful collaboration between the two countries on the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) project, which had made Ghana's electricity sector more resilient.

a1472.speaker: John Mahama, President-elect of Ghana
a1472.speech: also spoke on the need to collaborate more on security matters, given the challenges in the sub-region: "We know what the issues are in our sub-region, and the US has been a long-standing partner in terms of improving our resilience when it comes to security matters."

a1472.speaker: John Mahama, President-elect of Ghana
a1472.speech: highlighted his passion for agriculture and agribusiness and expressed his desire for knowledge sharing with the US to boost agriculture growth and food self-sufficiency in Ghana: "One of my passions is agriculture and agribusiness, we will see how we can share technology, share knowledge to boost the agriculture sector in Ghana."

a1472.speaker: Virginia E. Palmer, US Ambassador to Ghana
a1472.speech: congratulated Mr Mahama on his victory, saying, "My mission is to congratulate you in person" ; "I bring you greetings from President Biden, and you will be hearing directly from him," she said.

a1480.speaker: World Bank
a1480.speech: According to the World Bank, Lesotho faces a huge public debt dilemma in view of its small GDP. The bank puts the country’s public debt at M22.8 billion, with external debt accounting for 83 percent of this figure and domestic debt making up the remaining 17 percent.

a1480.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a1480.speech: Has projected a 100 percent increase in Lesotho’s public debt-to-GDP ratio, driven by the staggering global economic changes wrought by Mr Trump’s policies. The IMF notes that the increasing trade uncertainty, elevated geo-economic risks, spending pressures, and tighter financial conditions could further complicate Lesotho’s debt outlook by depressing growth and widening fiscal deficits.

a1480.speaker: Faizaan Kisat, IMF Fiscal Affairs Department
a1480.speech: Warned during the IMF’s Spring Meetings that debt levels are expected to keep rising for many countries, potentially approaching 100 percent of GDP by the end of the decade. He emphasized that “tackling debt risks should be a priority in many countries” as global public debt is projected to increase by 2.8 percentage points this year, more than double the estimates for 2024.

a1480.speaker: World Bank Group “Africa’s Pulse” report
a1480.speech: States that African countries heavily rely on external debt, but are constrained by weak tax policy and weak administrations that impede revenue collection. The report notes that “Weak institutional capacity in domestic revenue mobilization and heavy reliance on the extractives sector have exacerbated the debt burden in Sub-Saharan African countries.” It underscores the region’s heavy debt dependence, as “weak tax policy and administration continue to constrain revenue collection.” This challenge is further compounded by a large informal economy, where “nearly 90 percent of the labour force operates outside the formal tax net.”

a1480.speaker: Dr Retṧelisitsoe Nko, development finance specialist
a1480.speech: Warned that trade uncertainties spawned by US President Donald Trump’s chaotic tariff policies will likely force Lesotho to stretch its tax collection efforts to service its debt. As people move out of the formal economy, the government will have to divert more resources to cover the lost revenue, exacerbating the fiscal deficit, he said. This, he cautioned, could lead Lesotho to experiencing its own version of a “great depression” as the government is forced to prioritize debt repayment over supporting key economic areas.

a1480.speaker: Dr Retṧelisitsoe Nko, development finance specialist
a1480.speech: Notes that Lesotho’s heavy dependence on foreign aid has “prolonged a redundancy that has prevented the country from exploring opportunities to regenerate domestic income and production”, particularly in manufacturing and investment. He urges the government to convene a panel of experts to help it fundamentally change its economic mindset and “chart a path out of the crisis, before the country is dragged further down”.

a1480.speaker: Thabo Qhesi, Chief Executive Officer of the Private Sector Foundation of Lesotho (PSFL)
a1480.speech: Contends that Lesotho is likely to face difficulties in servicing its public debt and securing new loans from international creditors, because of the government’s approval of a national budget that did not account for the impact of new US tariffs. “These tariffs have slowed down trade, leading to reduced revenue collection, which adversely affects the budget,” Mr Qhesi said ; “Lesotho will not be able to service its public debt, and it may not be possible for the country to secure new loans,” he said.

a1480.speaker: Dr Moeketsi Majoro, former Prime Minister of Lesotho and former Minister of Finance and Development Planning
a1480.speech: Asserts it is not all doom and gloom for Lesotho. “Lesotho’s debt is not a significant problem,” he asserts. He explained that Lesotho had been consistently servicing its M23 billion debt in smaller instalments over the past 40 years as per contractual agreements with creditors like the World Bank and IMF. “External debt is not a problem for Lesotho,” Dr Majoro said. “Our national annual budget is about M20 billion, which is around 60 percent of the M23 billion debt. Additionally, we produce goods and services equivalent to 33 percent of our GDP each year, but the debt itself does not grow. We have a manageable timeline of up to 40 years to pay off the debt in small amounts.” ; Dr Majoro acknowledged that debt can become an issue if the economy collapses, and he expressed concern over the current signs of economic downturn in Lesotho and South Africa. However, he emphasized that Lesotho’s debt has been well-managed, allowing the country to avoid a debt crisis.

a1480.speaker: Dr Moeketsi Majoro, former Prime Minister of Lesotho
a1480.speech: Cautioned that excessive reliance on private sector debt, which often carries higher interest rates and shorter repayment periods, can be dangerous. In contrast, he said, Lesotho’s debt is primarily owed to multilateral institutions like the World Bank and IMF, which offer more favourable terms and longer repayment timelines. “The combination that makes debt very toxic is the infusion of too much private sector debt,” Dr Majoro said. “We are borrowing from the World Bank, IMF, and others, and the conditions are softer, and the terms are longer to repay. But negotiating a loan from the private sector can be much quicker, and the interest rates are much higher.”

a1480.speaker: Kamohelo Dooda, Central Bank of Lesotho (CBL) Economist, Research Department
a1480.speech: Emphasized that while the country is likely to be hit by trade uncertainties, Lesotho still has room to take on more loans and service the debt in the near future. “When we borrow, our debt increases. So, we have to look at our debt sustainability. In the Debt sustainability indicators, there are solvency and liquidity indicators. With solvency indicators we look at the sustainability of that debt level over a longer period, while liquidity is where we look at the government’s ability to honour its obligation and whether they are able to pay their debt,” Ms Dooda said. “The indicators have thresholds, which are alarms that you cannot go beyond a certain limit, as long as you are below those thresholds you are safe, but when you are beyond, your debt risk is not sustainable. Our GDP is going to be affected because we were exporting but now, we export less.” ; She added that as of March 2025, the threshold of external debt ratio to GDP is 40 percent, and “we are at 28.3 percent. This means we have a room to increase our debt without affecting our debt sustainability”. “This means Lesotho has the capacity to increase its debt, provided the funds are used to finance development,” she said ; “We don’t foresee a situation where we have a challenge to service our debt,” she said.

a1480.speaker: Kamohelo Dooda, Central Bank of Lesotho (CBL) Economist, Research Department
a1480.speech: Explained that if the economic performance of SACU member countries declined, leading to reduced trade, Lesotho would receive even less money from SACU. Furthermore, Ms Dooda said, if investors left due to struggling businesses and reduced exports, it would lead to job losses, decreased purchasing power, and lower tax revenues for the government. “When businesses struggle because they are exporting less, it means the government is going to get less income tax. Some people would lose their jobs, meaning the government will also lose personal income tax,” Ms Dooda said. She added that a decline in consumer spending would also result in a fall in VAT revenues. “We will see our revenues declining,” she warned ; “Our growth is going to be impacted, meaning we are going to have a problem with our GDP. Our numerator (debt) will increase, then our denominator, which is the GDP will decrease because the economy would be affected.”

a1573.speaker: Humanitarian community in South Sudan (press statement, 2025 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan launch)
a1573.speech: Appealed for US$1.7 billion to provide life-saving assistance to 5.4 million people experiencing the most acute needs across the country, and revealed that 9.3 million people – 69 per cent of South Sudan's total population of 13.4 million – are projected to require some form of humanitarian assistance in 2025.

a1573.speaker: Albino Akol Atak, Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management
a1573.speech: "Collaboration will continue in 2025 – not only to bring relief to people affected by crisis but also to support durable solutions and build their resilience by investing in the provision of basic services and livelihood opportunities to enable them to graduate from humanitarian assistance."

a1573.speaker: UN-OCHA (UN humanitarian agency)
a1573.speech: Said that since the outbreak of the Sudan crisis in April 2023, over 905,000 people have crossed into South Sudan, with an additional 337,000 people projected to arrive in 2025, and underlined that South Sudanese people continue to be affected by high levels of food insecurity and malnutrition.

a1573.speaker: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) report, released in November
a1573.speech: According to the report, 6.4 million people are severely food-insecure in crisis levels or worse (IPC Phase 3+), a number projected to increase to 7.7 million – over 57 per cent of the country's total population – during the lean season from April to July 2025.

a1573.speaker: Anita Kiki Gbeho, Humanitarian Coordinator for South Sudan
a1573.speech: "The 2025 HNRP paints an accurate picture of the most acute needs of vulnerable people across the country, and a plan for assistance that is realistic and most importantly, life-saving."

a1900.speaker: Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a1900.speech: Announced on 1 April that the Russian Ambassador to Niger and Mali, Igor Gromyko, took part in the ceremony handing over this humanitarian aid on 26 March in Niamey.

a1900.speaker: Representatives of the World Food Programme (WFP) present at the ceremony
a1900.speech: Indicated that this Russian aid would make it possible to "cover the needs of the most destitute populations, including refugees, in sunflower oil for a period of three months."

a1921.speaker: Experts (unnamed)
a1921.speech: warning of an escalating crisis in access to medical services and a potential brain drain, with an estimated 50,000 jobs at risk in Kenya's healthcare sector alone.

a2579.speaker: Daniel Ndoye, African Development Bank (AfDB) representative in Benin
a2579.speech: Said that one of the major challenges to be met in order to respond to the needs of traditionally underserved populations is the establishment of solid financial systems, noting that only 21% of adults on the continent have an account with formal financial institutions, and that the development of such financial systems in Africa is one of the important levers of AfDB action in achieving the objectives of its 2013-2022 ten-year strategy on inclusive growth; noted that the Patimf project fits well with this policy.

a2579.speaker: Valere Houssou, President of the Board of Directors of Consortium Alafia
a2579.speech: Said that transparency is not a gain but rather an objective to be approached daily by every actor, and cautioned that Patimf will not be limited solely to promoting price transparency in microfinance: "It will address more fully all the other elements of financial transparency, beginning with the regulatory framework applicable to decentralised financial systems (Sfd), their internal control system, the production of reliable information for the authority and for partners, external auditing, social performance management, promotion, and client protection." ; He went on that Apsfd-Benin, clients and the Business Development Service (Bds) Providers will also see their capacities strengthened so as to genuinely play their part in greater transparency within microfinance institutions.

a2579.speaker: Valere Houssou, President of the Board of Directors of Consortium Alafia
a2579.speech: Promised that all the required indicators would be met, and indicated that Consortium Alafia had successfully carried out, among others, the institutional strengthening project for the microfinance sector funded by USAID, the private sector development support project (Padsp) funded by the World Bank, and the MasterCard Foundation's Mission Africa project for the promotion of social performance management.

a2579.speaker: Jacques Dougnon, chief of staff of the minister in charge of Microfinance
a2579.speech: Said that these achievements attest to Consortium Alafia's constant presence alongside the decentralised financial systems (Sfd).

a2579.speaker: Alphonso Barnuevo, Ambassador of Spain, and Nicaise Tossou, national director for Benin and Togo of OIKO Credit
a2579.speech: Acknowledged the relevance and the interest of Patimf; like Spain through its ambassador, Oiko Credit also reaffirmed its readiness to support Consortium Alafia in the successful execution of the project.

a2684.speaker: Jacob Hara, Malawi Minister of Transport
a2684.speech: Confirmed that MCC has cancelled contracts for ongoing road works, blaming the development on the abrupt US policy shifts. He said: “The shutdown has affected the current funding as the MCC has communicated to us that they have now cancelled the contracts. We didn’t know about the shutdown in advance. MCA kept our hopes high that the MCC could survive the funding chop.” ; Said no road construction project gets backup donors, adding that government did not include the projects in the just-passed 2025-26 National Budget ; “We already had funding. We shall have to start from scratch looking for new financing.”

a2684.speaker: Grant Phillipp, public affairs officer, US Embassy in Lilongwe
a2684.speech: In an e-mailed response attributed the move to a federal directive. He said: “Under direction from the Department of Government Efficiency, a recommendation has been made that the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC), a US foreign assistance agency, wind down all programmes, including the MCC Malawi Transport and Land Compact. This recommendation will go to MCC’s Board for its decision on this recommendation.”

a2684.speaker: Reuters
a2684.speech: International media outlets like Reuters reported MCC’s impending closure due to US budget cuts. Reuters further reported that Kim told the staff that officials from Department of Government Efficiency headed by multi-billionaire Elon Musk visited MCC early last week and entered in talks with the leadership, who were attempting to save the agency.

a2684.speaker: Kyeh Kim, MCC senior official
a2684.speech: “Foreign aid is not a priority for the administration and so MCC’s work needs to wind down,” Reuters quoted MCC senior official Kyeh Kim as having told staff.

a2684.speaker: Millennium Challenge Account (Malawi) II Annual Recap official website
a2684.speech: Shows that the office began road construction under the Accelerated Growth Corridors Project in September 2024.

a2684.speaker: Mannes Nkhata, Farmers Union of Malawi president
a2684.speech: Has warned that rural farmers, especially women and persons with disabilities would suffer most from the shutdown.

a2924.speaker: Matthew Miller, US State Department spokesperson
a2924.speech: Said at a press conference: “We support their ability to strike militants and degrade Hezbollah’s infrastructure, but we are well aware of the many occasions in the past when Israel became involved in what appeared to be limited operations and remained for months or years” ; stressed that Washington wants the full implementation of UN Security Council resolution 1701, which among other points authorises an increase in the strength of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) to supervise the cessation of hostilities.

a2924.speaker: Matthew Miller, US State Department spokesperson
a2924.speech: Reiterated his government’s desire for a ceasefire and stressed that the cessation of hostilities cannot be unilateral: “We want a ceasefire that brings the hostages home, alleviates the suffering of the Palestinian people and allows humanitarian aid to reach Gaza” ; the United States also wants “an agreement on the political path forward that ensures that the Palestinians can elect their own leaders and that Hamas does not continue to reign as a terrorist organisation of Gaza over Gaza” ; “And, ultimately, that Gaza and the West Bank be reunified as an independent nation” ; “as long as Israel is mired in conflict in Gaza and as long as it is dealing with an unstable situation on its northern border and with unrest and insecurity in the West Bank, its security will never improve.”

a2924.speaker: Israeli Army (data released)
a2924.speech: At least 11 Israeli soldiers have died in combat since the ground operation began, according to data released by the Israeli Army.

a2924.speaker: Lebanese authorities
a2924.speech: The intense Israeli bombardments have already caused more than 2,000 deaths and one million displaced people, according to the Lebanese authorities.

a2980.speaker: Akinwumi A. Adesina, immediate-past African Development Bank (AfDB) president
a2980.speech: In the lecture, he said in the wake of a rapidly changing global landscape, time has come for Africa to wean itself from aid dependency and chart its future through self-reliance, strategic partnerships and exploiting its vast natural resources. ; "The era of aid or free money is gone. African countries must now learn to develop via investment discipline. Countries can no longer rely on aid for growth or count it as part of government revenue, as has been the case for decades. Benevolence is not an asset class."

a2980.speaker: The Nation (January 29 2025 edition)
a2980.speech: It was reported that $284.7 million (about K493.7 billion) financing through USAid to Malawi is at stake.

a2980.speaker: Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs (Malawi)
a2980.speech: Said of the amount, US contribution to the 2024/25 National Budget stood at K9.2 billion of the expected K1.17 trillion projected grants.

a2980.speaker: World Bank Group
a2980.speech: Describes trade as a golden key towards ending global poverty because countries that are open to international trade tend to grow faster, become innovative, improve productivity and provide higher income as well as more opportunities.

a3139.speaker: Luis Montiel, MSF emergency coordinator in Cabo Delgado
a3139.speech: On the current situation in Mocimboa: “Mocimboa da Praia is an important coastal town in northern Mozambique and the capital of a district with the same name. Prior to the conflict, it was a vibrant place with about 120,000 inhabitants, mostly dedicated to both artisanal and industrial fishing. The first attacks of the conflict in Cabo Delgado took place here in 2017. Later, violence hit the town very hard and it was taken over in 2020 by members of a non-state armed group. In August last year, Mozambican and Rwandese armed forces retook control of it. Today there is no active fighting in Mocimboa and there hasn’t been an incident for a long time, although the situation is volatile in neighbouring districts. The town is empty, without people living there. Administration officials regularly visit the area; the port is being dragged and services like electricity and water have been restored. But there is no trade and while the streets are mostly clean, some signs of the destruction are still visible.”

a3139.speaker: Luis Montiel, MSF emergency coordinator in Cabo Delgado
a3139.speech: On why MSF visited the town now: “We ran a medical project in Mocimboa throughout 2019 until March 2020, when we were forced to evacuate our teams as the place was being attacked. Even our office was partially burnt and occupied. This was the first time we returned since these events. We have been closely monitoring the situation and engaging with the different stakeholders to understand when community members may return. As we do in other parts of the province, MSF strives to adapt to the movements of people who flee conflict or who return home to areas after being displaced, to provide impartial medical and humanitarian assistance wherever the biggest needs are. We were informed by civilian authorities that several dozen people who had spent a long time in the bush were transferred by the security forces to Mocimboa after being set free by the non-state armed group... We were asked to do a mobile clinic to support people who stayed in the town. On 2 April, we sent a small team to Mocimboa for a one-day visit, during which we carried out consultations with 39 patients, mostly men and some teenagers and children as well. We didn’t find any critical medical issues and we only had to refer one patient who was suffering from cardiac problems to the Mueda rural hospital.”

a3139.speaker: Luis Montiel, MSF emergency coordinator in Cabo Delgado
a3139.speech: On MSF’s approach for the future: “People from Mocimboa town are still spread across different areas of Cabo Delgado... The route that connects Mocimboa northwards with Palma is already useable, but the route southwards towards Macomia is still unsafe. Through our work we know many displaced people from Mocimboa would like to return home, but for them to do so, the security is crucial, and a certain restoration of the economy is imperative. Our indicator to decide what medical support we can offer will be people and their needs. We are already running medical activities in some areas of Mocimboa district and will adapt activities in the district’s capital to people’s return. MSF will aim to provide community members with healthcare through mobile clinics and with other humanitarian assistance as needed. We have prepositioned some basic medical kits and our teams will start preparing to support people’s critical medical needs.”

a3139.speaker: Civilian authorities in Mocimboa da Praia (unnamed)
a3139.speech: informed MSF that several dozen people who had spent a long time in the bush were transferred by the security forces to Mocimboa after being set free by the non-state armed group, and asked MSF to do a mobile clinic to support people who stayed in the town.

a3153.speaker: Sir Keir Starmer, UK Prime Minister
a3153.speech: Told the House of Commons in February that the world had changed and rising security threats, particularly from Russia, required increased defence spending.

a3153.speaker: Colin Wells, British High Commissioner to Eswatini
a3153.speech: Confirmed the decision to cut bilateral development assistance to Eswatini to zero, describing it as “a difficult but necessary choice” in light of the UK’s security obligation ; “UK Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer made a difficult decision, reflecting the difficult security challenges around the threat from Russia.” ; “Looking ahead, we must modernise our approach towards development action, focusing on greater impact, ensuring every pound delivers for the UK taxpayer and the people we support overseas.”

a3153.speaker: Colin Wells, British High Commissioner to Eswatini
a3153.speech: Said that while Eswatini would no longer receive direct bilateral aid from the UK, it would continue to benefit through programmes run by multilateral partners ; “We will focus on three priorities in the future: humanitarian, health, climate and nature, underpinned by work to develop partners’ economies. Eswatini will continue to benefit from UK development spend through our multilateral partners like the UN and the World Bank.” ; expressed pride in the British High Commission’s previous bilateral initiatives in the country: “Sadly, our bilateral funds, which were already relatively small, have been reduced to zero in the current financial year. I am proud of the work that the British High Commission did to support community organisations. My team will continue to look creatively at how we can support that work in the future.” ; said the UK remains engaged with Eswatini and committed to supporting key areas of need.

a3153.speaker: Karsten Mecklenburg, European Union Ambassador to Eswatini
a3153.speech: Has cautioned that the ongoing war in Ukraine is consuming significant EU resources, many of which would otherwise support development initiatives in countries like Eswatini; said as the war enters its third year it is important to remember that it has far-reaching consequences even in countries geographically distant from the battlefield, and explained that while the EU is not a military participant it has been compelled to provide extensive support to Ukraine against what the EU describes as ‘Russia’s aggression’, with budgetary consequences for EU programming across Africa ; “We are affected, because we are now forced to support our partner Ukraine. Tremendous resources are being absorbed by this unnecessary illegal war and these resources are not anymore at our disposal to work with other countries.” ; added that although the EU remains committed to its partnerships, it has already had to adjust programming volumes and may be forced to reduce further if the war continues: “We want to continue with our programming with Eswatini and other partners in Africa, but we had already reduced and adapted our volume. And if this goes on, we will be forced to do that further, because we can only spend the money we have.”

a3173.speaker: Bintou Keita, head of the United Nations peace mission in the DRC (MONUSCO)
a3173.speech: drew an alarming picture before the UN Security Council of the evolution of the conflict and the absence of progress in implementing the ceasefire: "Despite significant regional and international efforts, the immediate and unconditional ceasefire called for by the East African Community, the Southern African Development Community, the African Union, Security Council resolution 2773 and, more recently, under the auspices of Qatar, has still not materialised."

a3173.speaker: Bintou Keita, head of the United Nations peace mission in the DRC (MONUSCO)
a3173.speech: denounced the increase in sexual violence and the forced recruitment of children into armed groups, aggravating an already dramatic humanitarian crisis.

a3173.speaker: Bintou Keita, head of the United Nations peace mission in the DRC (MONUSCO)
a3173.speech: also warned about the impact of the freeze on American funding on humanitarian aid, calling for a rethink of intervention models in order to help local associations.

a3173.speaker: Democratic Republic of Congo (government)
a3173.speech: denounces the M23's establishment of a parallel administration as a direct attack on its sovereignty.

a3173.speaker: Zenon Mukongo Ngay, permanent representative of the DRC to the UN
a3173.speech: reacted firmly: "The right to self-defence cannot be invoked as justification for an armed invasion, nor for the creation of parallel administrations on the territories of a sovereign State. These facts in themselves constitute serious violations of the Charter of the United Nations."

a3173.speaker: Rwanda (government)
a3173.speech: continues to reject the accusations of support for the M23 and defends its position by asserting that it is only taking defensive measures to secure its border with the DRC.

a3173.speaker: Olivier Nduhungirehe, Rwandan Minister of Foreign Affairs
a3173.speech: declared: "Why is Rwanda being targeted in a disproportionate manner? What is certain for us, in Rwanda, is that the defensive measures we have put in place will remain in place until security along our border with the DRC can be guaranteed in a credible and long-term manner."

a3173.speaker: United Nations / MONUSCO
a3173.speech: insist on the need to take concrete action to sanction those responsible for human rights violations ; the organisation also insists on the need to reopen the airports of Goma and Kavumu in order to facilitate humanitarian operations.

a3200.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) (statement)
a3200.speech: Said on Friday that the floods have affected about 1.4 million people across 43 counties and the disputed Abyei region, which is claimed by both South Sudan and Sudan, and added that more than 379,000 people were displaced in 22 counties and in Abyei ; “A surge in malaria has been reported in Jonglei, Unity, Upper Nile, Northern Bahr el Ghazal, Central Equatoria and Western Equatoria states – overwhelming the health system and exacerbating the situation and impact in flood-hit areas.”

a3200.speaker: Aid agencies
a3200.speech: Have said the world's youngest country, highly vulnerable to climate change, is in the grip of its worst flooding in decades, mainly in the north.

a3200.speaker: The World Bank
a3200.speech: Said last month that the latest floods were “worsening an already critical humanitarian situation marked by severe food insecurity, economic decline, continued conflict, disease outbreaks, and the repercussions of the Sudan conflict”.

a3200.speaker: UN World Food Programme
a3200.speech: More than seven million people are food insecure in South Sudan and 1.65 million children are malnourished, according to the UN's World Food Programme.

a3200.speaker: Office of the President of South Sudan
a3200.speech: Announced in September yet another extension to a transitional period agreed to in a 2018 peace deal, delaying elections by two years to December 2026.

a3222.speaker: Sophia Akuffo, Former Chief Justice of Ghana and Council of State member
a3222.speech: Has criticised the process that led to the removal of Chief Justice Gertrude Araba Esaaba Sackey Torkornoo, stating that her successor was not given a fair hearing and insisting that the allegations that led to the removal were not strong enough to justify her dismissal by President John Dramani Mahama; described the impeachment as troubling for the independence of the judiciary and condemned the dismissal, describing the proceedings as a "rigmarole" that set a dangerous precedent for Ghana's judiciary ; "She did not get a fair trial. Even though it is not a trial strictly speaking, it was handled as though it were a treason trial" (told TV3 in an interview) ; "They lack the gravity that will lead to a grave outcome, such as the removal of the head of an institution of justice" ; "The [allegations] lack the gravity that will lead to a grave outcome such as the removal of the head of an institution of justice."

a3222.speaker: Sophia Akuffo, Former Chief Justice of Ghana and Council of State member
a3222.speech: Urged the ousted Chief Justice to remain strong and trust in God during what she described as a difficult and unfair ordeal: "She should take heart. That God sees, and sometimes when you go through certain things which you think have brought you to the end or to your knees or something like that, that could be far from the truth" ; "There could be bigger, better and greater needs that the Lord has in store. That is what I will tell her, and that is what I will send to her as a text message" ; "When you are a believer, things happen today, yes, they have happened, so look to God and move on, and you will allow God to manage the rest."

a3222.speaker: Sophia Akuffo, JSC (in the Supreme Court ruling in Awuni v West African Examination Council)
a3222.speech: Stated: "... In my view, the scope of article 23 is such that, there is not distinction made between acts done in exercise of ordinary administrative functions and quasi-judicial administrative function.. Where a body or officer has an administrative function to perform, the activity must be conducted with and reflect the qualities of fairness, reasonableness and legal compliance. I will not venture to give a comprehensive definition of what is fair and reasonable, since these qualities are dictated by the circumstances in which the administrative function is performed. At the very least, however, it includes probity, transparency, objectivity opportunity to be heard, legal competence and absence of bias, caprice or ill-will. In particular, whereas in this case, the likely outcome of an administrative activity is of Penal nature, no matter how strong the suspicion of the commission of the offence, it is imperative that all affected persons be given reasonable notice of the allegations against them and reasonable opportunity to be heard, if the objective of Article 23 is to be achieved."

a3222.speaker: Supreme Court panel presided over by Justice Akuffo in Agyei Twum v Attorney General & Akwetey (ruling)
a3222.speech: Made it clear that the Chief Justice's administrative acts are not immune from the impeachment process; Justice Akuffo was quoted alongside Dr Samuel Date-Bah, JSC, and the late Prof. Justice Tawuah Modibo Ocran, JSC, making this clear, and the ruling was cited in the petition of Daniel Ofori.

a3222.speaker: Prof. Justice Tawuah Modibo Ocran, JSC (in Agyei Twum v Attorney General & Akwetey)
a3222.speech: Expressed that "A claim of constitutionally protected absolute administrative autonomy for the Chief Justice must fail."

a3222.speaker: Dr Samuel Date-Bah, JSC (in Agyei Twum v Attorney General & Akwetey)
a3222.speech: Stated at page 751 that the Chief Justice's acts must comply with the provisions of Article 296 of the Constitution: "Rather, what is relevant is the Chief Justice's implied duty to be fair and candid in the exercise of his discretionary power, as laid down in Article 296 of the Constitution."

a3222.speaker: The Herald (newspaper's own findings)
a3222.speech: The Herald's findings saw Justice Akuffo eating back her words while commenting on the dismissal; The Herald learnt that Lawyer Okudzeto in particular was allowed to talk and talk, and was left surprised when the lawyers of Petitions decided not to cross-examine him.

a3222.speaker: Article 146 Committee of Inquiry (chaired by Justice Gabriel Scott Pwamang) / petition of Daniel Ofori
a3222.speech: Justice Torkornoo faced the Committee on an arbitrary decision, flagrant disregard for court orders, and abuse of office, including summoning court officials into her office and directing them on what to do with respect to people's cases; she was accused of having misappropriated GHS 261,890.00 of public funds in 2023 for the benefit of her private foreign travel with her husband and daughter and US$30,000 in per diem allowance, of misappropriating GHS75,580.00 of public funds for Ethiopian Airlines tickets for herself and her husband during their vacation to Arusha, Tanzania, and of obtaining an accountable imprest of $14,000.00 to travel with her husband to Arusha, Tanzania, which she failed to retire.

a3222.speaker: Witnesses for Justice Torkornoo (Ex-Chief Justice Kwasi Ani-Yeboah, Justice Jones Dotse, Nana Dr. SKB Asante, Lawyer Samuel Okudzeto and others)
a3222.speech: Testified in Justice Torkornoo's favour; they were said to have spoken about Justice Gertrude Torkornoo's character and not the issues against her, including abuse of office and misappropriation of funds, among others.

a3222.speaker: Government of Ghana
a3222.speech: The government maintained it was constitutionally mandated to act on the committee's findings.

a3222.speaker: Presidency of Ghana (statement signed by Felix Kwakye Ofosu, Spokesperson to the President and Minister for Government Communications)
a3222.speech: A statement from the Presidency said the decision followed a recommendation by a committee set up under Article 146(6) to investigate a petition filed by a citizen, Mr. Daniel Ofori, and that the removal took immediate effect; the statement noted that the President was constitutionally bound to act in line with the committee's recommendation.

a3222.speaker: Gertrude Torkornoo, dismissed Chief Justice of Ghana
a3222.speech: Had earlier described the process as "cruel" and unconstitutional.

a3222.speaker: Alfred Tuah-Yeboah, former Deputy Attorney General
a3222.speech: Weighed in, calling the removal an "unholy assault on the independence of the judiciary" and a fulfilment of a campaign promise by the current administration.

a3256.speaker: United Nations (UN)
a3256.speech: Said on Monday 30 October that 6.9 million people are currently displaced inside the Democratic Republic of Congo, notably because of the resurgence of violence in the east of the country.

a3256.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM) (statement)
a3256.speech: In its statement, stresses that a large majority of the displaced need humanitarian aid.

a3380.speaker: Hibo Mohamed Muse, national coordinator of the GEF Small Grants Programme
a3380.speech: During her presentation, encouraged all associations to submit quality projects meeting the programme’s eligibility conditions in the environmental field ; mentioned that a new call for proposals had been published in the columns of the newspaper “La Nation”, closing on 13 April, intended for associations working in the regions to submit projects combating climate change or ensuring the protection of the environment.

a3380.speaker: Dini Abdallah Omar, Secretary General of the Ministry of Housing, Urban Planning and the Environment (MHUE)
a3380.speech: In his opening remarks to the workshop, stressed that this programme constituted a real funding opportunity for community projects, adding that despite the efforts deployed there still appears to be a weakness in project submission, an absence of synergy in the actions undertaken and in the mobilisation of available financial resources: “That is why this awareness-raising workshop is a necessary exercise to provide information on the ins and outs of this programme, with a view to supporting associations in formulating bankable projects and gaining easier access to financing. You will be presented with the elements of information inherent to the GEF’s policies, missions and procedures as well as the SGP’s funding opportunities.”

a3380.speaker: Fatima ElSheik, UNDP Resident Representative in Djibouti
a3380.speech: Said the UNDP and the UN play a leading role in defining the guiding principles of environmental governance and achieving the Millennium Development Goals, particularly the 7th MDG on environmental preservation, and that the Djiboutian government’s effort in subscribing to this objective counts for a great deal ; said the programme is the happy outcome of a process begun in 2007 by the Ministry of Housing, Urban Planning and the Environment and the result of long cooperation between the UNDP, the GEF and the ministry, calling it “one more victory for the environment in Djibouti”.

a3380.speaker: Fatima ElSheik, UNDP Resident Representative in Djibouti
a3380.speech: Said that globally the programme counts more than 14,500 projects in more than 125 countries since 1992, and that in Djibouti 20 associations received funding between 2013 and 2018 ; said that despite the limited amount of each grant (a maximum of 50,000 dollars) the programme has achieved considerable concrete results in all countries, and that as independent evaluations have revealed it has produced tangible results in terms of capacity building with effects on the ground, citing ecosystem restoration, construction of wells and reservoirs and installation of solar panels, with 60% of projects targeting destitute populations.

a3380.speaker: Fatima ElSheik, UNDP Resident Representative in Djibouti
a3380.speech: “I am convinced that this programme will make it possible to establish an appropriate framework for supporting communities in their own initiatives aimed at securing sustainable livelihoods in Djibouti” ; reiterated the UNDP’s commitment to support all the efforts of the government, the associations and the grassroots communities aimed at strengthening the resilience of Djibouti’s rural communities.

a3432.speaker: Kathleen Addy, Chairperson of the National Commission for Civic Education (NCCE)
a3432.speech: Has called on the youth of Madina to make wise and informed choices in the upcoming 2024 general elections; emphasised the importance of civic responsibility, urging young people to reject violence, misinformation, and electoral misconduct; highlighted the role of responsible decision-making in shaping Ghana's future ; "We are here to help you understand the importance of peaceful elections. This engagement aims to prepare you to make informed choices as you elect our next leaders."

a3432.speaker: Kathleen Addy, Chairperson of the National Commission for Civic Education (NCCE)
a3432.speech: Identified key issues, including the rising use of inflammatory language, the spread of fake news, religious intolerance, and the growing trend of monetization in politics ; "We want you to resist the temptation of violence and misinformation. Let your actions reflect a commitment to peace and respect for our democratic values." ; encouraged the youth to steer clear of violence and avoid being influenced by those who promote aggression as a means to support political parties: "Fighting does not attract votes. It only makes your party unattractive," she warned, adding that acts of violence have lasting consequences, both legally and personally.

a3432.speaker: Kathleen Addy, Chairperson of the National Commission for Civic Education (NCCE)
a3432.speech: Stressed the significance of Ghana's Public Order Act, reminding attendees that misconduct during elections comes with legal repercussions: "Understand that there are implications for actions done illegally. Respect for law and order is fundamental to a peaceful election."

a3432.speaker: Kathleen Addy, Chairperson of the National Commission for Civic Education (NCCE)
a3432.speech: "We want you to be ambassadors for the NCCE, sharing these values with family, friends, and community members."

a3440.speaker: António Guterres, United Nations Secretary-General
a3440.speech: Once again demanded a ceasefire in the Gaza Strip and an end to the Russia-Ukraine war; before the BRICS and other guests at the group's sixteenth summit in Kazan he again demanded peace and a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine: "We need peace in Ukraine, a just peace in accordance with the United Nations Charter, international law and General Assembly resolutions. We need peace in Sudan, with all parties silencing their weapons and committing to a path to sustainable peace." ; on the Middle East: "We need peace in Gaza with an immediate ceasefire, the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, the effective delivery of humanitarian aid without obstacles. And we need to make irreversible progress towards ending the occupation and establishing the two-State solution, as was recently reaffirmed, once again, by a resolution of the United Nations General Assembly."

a3440.speaker: António Guterres, United Nations Secretary-General
a3440.speech: Reminded the group of nine and their guests of the need for global inclusion, lamenting the levels of hunger and poverty in the world: "No group and no country can act alone or in isolation. What is needed is a community of nations working as a global family to confront global challenges. Challenges such as the growing number of conflicts, the devastation caused by climate change, pollution and biodiversity loss, rising inequalities and the persistence of poverty and hunger, compound the crises that threaten the future plans of many vulnerable countries."

a3440.speaker: Vladimir Putin, President of Russia
a3440.speech: In the closing speech of the meeting, which ended with several agreements among members, said he was open to any options for ending the war in Ukraine.

a3707.speaker: Seydou Asman, Minister of Trade and Industry of Niger
a3707.speech: Praised the quality of the cement produced at the Badaguichiri plant and suggested making it more accessible on the market, notably by reducing the price in order to face competition ; at the Malbaza cement plant (MCC), after a meeting with the plant's officials, recommended making cement accessible to everyone and at lower cost.

a3756.speaker: Experts and pre-school practitioners (unanimous)
a3756.speech: “Play helps the child to get along well with others, to share, to wait his turn and to follow rules. Playing also allows him to communicate, to experiment and to find solutions to problems.”

a3756.speaker: Practitioners and pedagogues specialising in teaching and learning
a3756.speech: Affirm far and wide that when a child has fun, he feels good and joyful, which facilitates learning ; “Playing therefore allows him to develop a positive attitude towards school. That is why nursery-school teaching leaves a good place for play, because play allows the child to develop his knowledge by exploring. As he is having fun, it gives him a taste for learning and for making an effort.”

a3756.speaker: Head of the Play to Learn project
a3756.speech: Outlined in broad strokes the objectives and the activities included in this four-year project: strengthening the national strategy for the development of pre-school education to 100% for children aged 5 by 2030, improving access to equitable, safe and inclusive pre-school education services, strengthening the quality of those services and fostering an environment that strengthens the system of services capable of developing early childhood.

a3756.speaker: Andrea Tomasziewics, Chargée d'Affaires of the US Embassy in Djibouti
a3756.speech: Indicated that the objective of the project is to support the efforts of the Government of Djibouti to improve equitable and quality access to education for children aged three to six ; “We are proud of the strong partnership that USAID has built with the Government of Djibouti since its beginnings, and which has benefited all Djiboutians.”

a3756.speaker: Moustapha Mohamed Mahamoud, Minister of National Education and Vocational Training of Djibouti
a3756.speech: Indicated that the Play to Learn project comes at a moment when MENFOP is consolidating its gains and strengthening its actions, all the more so as its approach covers the whole early-childhood pathway, from nursery to pre-school, and gives MENFOP and the Ministry of Women and the Family the opportunity to think about this educational offer together and coherently.

a3756.speaker: Mouna Osman Aden, Minister of Women and the Family of Djibouti
a3756.speech: For her part emphasised the value of the Play to Learn project, which will provide facilitation tools for the holistic development of early childhood ; thanked USAID for this project, which comes at just the right time to revitalise all the community childcare structures and solve the problem of the motivation of the staff of those structures.

a3756.speaker: Ayane Osman Abrar, Technical Adviser and Executive Secretary of the Higher Committee for Education
a3756.speech: Shared her experience of a timely visit she made to the United States of America to learn about pre-school education systems.

a4015.speaker: Nasir Abujaish, Palestinian Ambassador to Ethiopia
a4015.speech: Asked for support from other countries in opposing the recent shift of the American Embassy to Jerusalem: “We saw that some countries who were opposed to moving the US Embassy to the occupied Jerusalem territory attended the celebration in Jerusalem and witness the move of the US embassy. This is unfair” he said in a briefing on Tuesday, May 15.

a4015.speaker: Nasir Abujaish, Palestinian Ambassador to Ethiopia
a4015.speech: Asked whether shifting the US embassy to Jerusalem will motivate others to do the same thing: “I don’t think so, but if they will do that we will oppose it because we will not accept Jerusalem without Palestine.”

a4015.speaker: Nasir Abujaish, Palestinian Ambassador to Ethiopia
a4015.speech: Said that the ongoing massacre in the Gaza Strip which happened last week was planned in advance, since the protests began on March 30 ; “The Israeli officials and the American president and his advisor are accountable for committing war crimes against the defenseless Palestine people. Many times we warned that President Trump’s decision will have repercussions on the stability of the region in particular and the world in general. It will also expand the cycle of violence in the world and in the Middle East region, especially its impact on the spiritual, cultural and historical status of the Holy City in the Islamic and Christian conscience.”

a4015.speaker: Ethiopia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a4015.speech: Said despite media reports, its delegates did not participate in the opening celebrations of the US embassy in Jerusalem.

a4015.speaker: Meles Alem, MoFA spokesperson
a4015.speech: In a statement clarified that media reports indicating Ethiopia as one of the African countries which were planning to participate in the event were not true.

a4015.speaker: Haaretz, leading Israeli daily newspaper (report)
a4015.speech: First reported the news that Ethiopia, Nigeria and Thailand were among the countries attending the opening ceremony.

a4015.speaker: Nigeria and Thailand (official statements)
a4015.speech: Have also issued statements saying their delegates were not part of the opening ceremony.

a4015.speaker: The Trump administration
a4015.speech: Has said the city’s final borders should be decided by the parties.

a4038.speaker: Leonce Ndakumana, Burundian Professor of Economics at the University of Massachusetts Amherst
a4038.speech: Has studied the Politics of Aid and found that in fact, instead of being a net recipient of Aid, as it is said, Africa is a net creditor to America and the world through its corrupt leaders.

a4038.speaker: ActionAid study 'Real Aid'
a4038.speech: Studies by Action Aid called Real Aid reached similar conclusions - that on the surface and in the short run America may appear to provide Aid to most of the world, but it reaps out bigger sheaths, so it will suffer too.

a4129.speaker: Jim Stewart, Chief Operating Officer of Onne Multipurpose Terminal (OMT)
a4129.speech: Praised the Managing Director of the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA), Dr. Abubakar Dantsoho, for supporting and improving port efficiency, saying the Authority under his watch has been instrumental to the successes of the terminal; expressed appreciation to the NPA for its vital support in creating an enabling environment for OMT to thrive: “We have an excellent working relationship with the Onne Port Manager, Mr. Abdulrahmon Hussain, and the entire team at the Nigerian Ports Authority. The leadership of the Managing Director, Dr. Abubakar Dantsoho, has been instrumental in our success. Allowing a vessel of this magnitude to berth at our terminal is a vote of confidence in our capabilities.”

a4129.speaker: Jim Stewart, Chief Operating Officer of Onne Multipurpose Terminal (OMT)
a4129.speech: Called on the Federal Government to allocate more funding for channel dredging at the Onne Port to accommodate even larger vessels and further boost trade volumes: “We are fully prepared to receive vessels from any shipping line. But for us to unlock the full potential of Onne Port, additional dredging is essential. We urge the Federal Government to support NPA with the necessary resources to deepen and widen the channels.”

a4129.speaker: Jim Stewart, Chief Operating Officer of Onne Multipurpose Terminal (OMT)
a4129.speech: Described the vessel call at OMT as a landmark event not only for the terminal but for Nigeria’s maritime industry at large: “We are incredibly honoured to receive the largest vessel to ever berth at Onne.
