The 2024 WHO Global Tuberculosis Report reveals that Nigeria recorded approximately 467,000 TB cases in 2023, underscoring the urgent need for collective action" ; "The solution lies in the strength of partnerships between public and private sectors, alongside integrated service delivery that ensures no one is left behind."

a7318.speaker: Oluremi Tinubu, First Lady of Nigeria
a7318.speech: Acknowledged strides made in diagnosing and treating TB, attributing them to the Federal Government's Renewed Hope Agenda under President Bola Tinubu, along with support from civil society organizations and international partners such as USAID and the Global Fund.

a7318.speaker: Oluremi Tinubu, First Lady of Nigeria
a7318.speech: Reaffirmed her dedication to eradicating TB, sharing that her previous donation had been used to acquire diagnostic tools, enhance case detection, and improve other vital services; and praised the conference as a vital platform for exchanging knowledge, developing strategies, and renewing the commitment to combating TB.

a7318.speaker: 2024 WHO Global Tuberculosis Report
a7318.speech: Reveals that Nigeria recorded approximately 467,000 TB cases in 2023.

a7357.speaker: Ben Nangombe, Executive Director of the Ministry of Health and Social Services
a7357.speech: reiterated that Namibia has made commendable progress in curbing the spread of infectious diseases like HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria: “We have witnessed significant forward movement in achieving the goals articulated in the National Strategic Framework, thanks in large part to the invaluable support by our Development Cooperation Partners and the active role of Civil Society Organisations (CSOs). The data and figures towards Namibia’s achievements of the UNAIDS 95-95-95 fast-tracked targets for HIV are well known to all of you. As of 2022 in Namibia, 94% of HIV-positive individuals know their status, 97% of them are on antiretroviral therapy (ART), and 93% have reached viral suppression (94-97-93).”

a7357.speaker: Ben Nangombe, Executive Director of the Ministry of Health and Social Services
a7357.speech: “This is the last mile, and we dare not relent. We will not falter. Not now, when we have achieved so much. Let us maintain the momentum and deliver a solid NOP and a comprehensive sustainability framework to operationalise our NSF for HIV, TB, malaria, and hepatitis.”

a7357.speaker: Cheryl Amoroso, PEPFAR Representative
a7357.speech: discussed the funding perspective of PEPFAR as a donor: “From a PEPFAR perspective, we need to already embrace change to together understand the transformation of HIV programming in line with this developing vision that the country has for its future health system, not just from an HIV perspective but holistically. From a donor viewpoint, we are ready to adapt our investments to help realise this developing vision, which is why today and tomorrow are so important. We will use this roadmap to guide our investment. The Namibia PEPFAR investments have already started making shifts better aligned with the future vision that is already developing, and the clarity that we will have on this documentation will continue to support that transition.”

a7428.speaker: Najib Abdallah Kamil, Secretary General of the Presidency of the Council of Ministers (Prime Minister’s Office) of Djibouti
a7428.speech: Delivered a brief speech at the opening session of the meeting in which he affirmed our country’s determination to strengthen synergy among the various stakeholders, to enhance cooperation and avoid duplication of projects, which would improve the impact of our collective efforts and make our monitoring mechanism more efficient, noting that this meeting constitutes an opportunity to discuss the challenges, opportunities and issues relating to priority projects and to the effectiveness of coordination.

a7494.speaker: Federal officials of Ethiopia
a7494.speech: Have unveiled a three-pronged allocation strategy for this year’s anticipated avocado bonanza: of the record 18.1 million tonnes forecasted, half is earmarked for export, 40pc for domestic consumption, and the balance for industrial processing.

a7494.speaker: Mohammedsani Amin, deputy head of the Oromia Bureau of Agriculture
a7494.speech: “We’ve plans to export most of the avocado harvest. Production is scaling up as we collect avocados from smallholder farmers organised in clusters.”

a7494.speaker: Ministry of Agriculture survey
a7494.speech: Pegs domestic demand at roughly 80,000tns a year, a reminder that market knowledge is thin.

a7494.speaker: Mohammedsani Amin, deputy head of the Oromia Bureau of Agriculture
a7494.speech: “We currently export only one of the seven varieties we grow,” noting that foreign buyers want fruit that most growers do not yet produce in quantity.

a7494.speaker: Abayneh Melkie, researcher at Debre Markos University
a7494.speech: “Farmers don’t know how to handle avocados after harvest. This contributes to quality loss.” He urged government-led awareness drives, more investment in refrigerated transport, expanded cultivation of export-friendly varieties and better packaging.

a7494.speaker: Mengistu Tesfaye, manager of Southern Ethiopia’s Kayu Fruits & Vegetables Cooperative Union
a7494.speech: “Seedlings are expensive, and the current varieties need heavy watering and compost. We also don’t have enough variety to meet market needs.”

a7494.speaker: Mengistu Tesfaye, manager of Kayu Fruits & Vegetables Cooperative Union
a7494.speech: Said intermediaries often dump ripe and unripe fruit together in flimsy sacks, bruising the crop. “It ruins the fruit and sometimes damages future harvests.” He also said the Union has sold 55,000Kg this year, including 33,000Kg to a company operating in one of the industrial parks, and hopes to hit 70,000Kg by December.

a7494.speaker: Wale Getaneh, project coordinator at the Ethiopian Horticulture Producer Exporters Association
a7494.speech: “Our exports have grown from eight to 14tns in two years.”

a7494.speaker: Wale Getaneh, project coordinator at the Ethiopian Horticulture Producer Exporters Association
a7494.speech: “I advise the private sector to invest in avocado exports. The government should offer incentives to make this sector attractive.”

a7494.speaker: Rahewa Mohammed, avocado exporter
a7494.speech: “Payment issues and amendments are my biggest challenges. Sometimes, I ship 4,000Kg but receive less than that. I don’t find out until it arrives.” She said it takes months for her to settle the difference, that she risks losing her investment if anything goes wrong, and that at times she is not paid at all.

a7494.speaker: Elias Gulilat, former avocado exporter
a7494.speech: Left the business after a year; his Turkish buyer came to Ethiopia but left empty-handed because he did not get the variety he wanted. “Even worse, we shipped to people who disappeared after receiving our produce.”

a7494.speaker: Zekarias Assefa, deputy secretary-general, Addis Abeba Chamber of Commerce & Sectoral Associations
a7494.speech: Said the Chamber steps in by contacting embassies or foreign chambers to track down errant buyers.

a7494.speaker: Backers of the new strategy
a7494.speech: Say it can work if every link in the chain — from nurseries to shipping lines — tightens up.
